topic: the WWI fatigue study that accidentally won the 8-hour workday
title: The WWI Study That Accidentally Won The 8-Hour Workday
description: The 8-hour workday wasn't handed over out of kindness -- a wartime study on tired factory workers is what actually changed employers' minds. AI-narrated commentary, original script.

hook_candidates.text: Working longer shifts once made factories produce less work overall.
Why did some of history's most stubborn factory owners suddenly beg workers to work fewer hours?
The 8-hour workday wasn't won by picket signs -- it was won by a stopwatch.
In 1915, Britain pushed munitions workers to 12-hour shifts to win a war, then panicked at the numbers.

payoff_mechanism: Past roughly eight to ten hours, fatigue makes workers slower and more error-prone per hour, so the extra hours actually produce less added output than they cost in mistakes, injuries, and slowed pace, making a shorter shift more productive overall.

beats.text: Working **longer** shifts once made factories produce **less**.
WWI Britain pushed munitions workers to **12-hour** days to win faster.
Past **ten** hours, fatigue caused mistakes that erased the extra output.
So shifts dropped to **eight**, and output jumped. Follow for more hidden history.
